cards.def: An Old English epic poem about a Geatish hero who fights the monster Grendel, Grendel's mother, and a dragon.
A long narrative poem about a hero whose great deeds decide the fate of a whole people.
A great wooden hall where a lord feasted his warriors, gave them treasure, and sheltered them, making it the center of a tribe's life.
A kenning for a king, who earns his warriors' loyalty by handing out rings and treasure.
A warrior who serves a lord in exchange for the lord's protection and gifts.
A sworn follower who lives in a lord's household and fights for him.
The bond between a chief and his war-band, in which he gives protection and treasure and they give loyalty to the death.
An Old English court poet who composed and sang stories of heroes to the harp in the mead-hall.
A short narrative song performed by a poet about a hero or a famous event.
A compound metaphor that names a thing by describing it, like "whale-road" for the sea.
A kenning for the sea, pictured as the road that whales travel.
A kenning for the sea, pictured as the path on which swans ride.
A kenning for the sea, pictured as a huge tub of waves.
A kenning for a person's store of words, so "unlocked his word-hoard" means he began to speak.
A kenning for a mail shirt, the woven net of iron rings that covers the chest.
A kenning for a shield, the wooden board carried into battle.
A kenning for Grendel that pictures him as a creature who hunts under cover of darkness.
A kenning for Grendel that pictures him as a creature who lurks around Heorot waiting to strike.
A descriptive phrase attached to a name, like "protector of the Shieldings," that tells what a person is known for.
Varied epithets for the Danes that praise them for their skill in war, their wealth, and their glory.
The repetition of the same first sound in nearby stressed words, which binds each line of Old English poetry together in place of rhyme.
A pause in the middle of an Old English line that splits it into two half-lines linked by alliteration.
A formal public vow in which a warrior names the deed he will do and stakes his honor on doing it.
A ritual contest of insults and counter-boasts between two warriors.
A payment made to a victim's family that settles a killing and replaces blood revenge.
Another name for wergild, the payment owed to a dead man's kin to end a feud.
A cycle of revenge killings between families or tribes that lasts until compensation is paid or one side is destroyed.
The Old English idea of fate, a fixed destiny that decides how each person's life will end.
The warrior ethic that demands courage, loyalty to one's lord, revenge for slain kin, and deeds that win lasting fame.
The lasting reputation a warrior wins through his deeds, the only part of him that outlives death in the heroic world.
A guardian entrusted with defending a lord's hall.
A heavy twisted metal ring worn around the neck as a sign of wealth and rank.
Body armor made of small interlocking iron rings that keeps blades from cutting through.
A boar image mounted on a helmet as a charm believed to protect the wearer.
An abandoned child who is found and raised by strangers.
A funeral in which a dead lord is laid in a ship loaded with treasure and sent out to sea.
Ironic understatement that stresses a point by denying its opposite, like "it was hardly a shame to be showered with such gifts."
A story inside the main story that comments on the main action through comparison or contrast.
A hint of a later event that builds a sense of coming doom.
The poem's name for the monsters descended from Cain, whom God cursed and exiled for murdering his brother Abel.
An Irish-English word for the fortified yard around a hall.
A drinking celebration with toasts.
